paragraphs: This paper studies repeated trade between a seller and a buyer when their private valuations can vary arbitrarily, as if chosen by an adversary. The mechanism seeks to maximize gains from trade while making truthful participation worthwhile and keeping its budget balanced. Its objective is specifically gains from trade, which the authors identify as harder to approximate than social welfare.

The analysis compares what becomes possible under different feedback and pricing rules. Alpha-regret measures performance against an approximation-adjusted benchmark; sublinear regret means the accumulated shortfall grows slower than the number of rounds. The authors show that achieving this is impossible for any approximation factor below two, whereas full feedback permits sublinear regret at factor two.

With partial feedback, a single posted price cannot achieve sublinear alpha-regret for any constant factor. Allowing separate buyer and seller prices changes the result: even one bit of feedback permits sublinear two-regret. Full and partial feedback still have provably different two-regret bounds. The findings establish that pricing flexibility can fundamentally change what limited information allows.
neurips-2022-an-alpha-regret-analysis-of.tldr: Separate buyer and seller prices enable sublinear two-regret with minimal feedback in adversarial bilateral trade, while a single price cannot.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of vertices, making their higher-order structure central to learning useful representations. This paper studies how contrastive learning can improve hypergraph neural networks when labels are scarce. Its main question is how to create augmented views that support learning while retaining information useful for downstream tasks.

The proposed HyperGCL approach explores both designed and learned augmentations. The authors construct two hyperedge augmentation schemes using domain knowledge and adapt three vertex augmentation strategies from graph learning. They also introduce a generative hypergraph model that produces augmented views. A differentiable training pipeline allows these augmentations and the neural network parameters to be learned together.

In the experiments, hyperedge changes provide the largest gains among the designed augmentations, suggesting that higher-order structure is often especially relevant to downstream predictions. Generative augmentations preserve that information better and further improve generalization. The authors also report improvements in robustness and fairness. These findings make view construction a substantive modeling choice, rather than merely a preparatory step before contrastive training.
neurips-2022-augmentations-in-hypergraph.tldr: HyperGCL improves learning with scarce labels by designing or learning hypergraph augmentations that preserve useful higher-order relationships.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select among nested policy classes in contextual bandit problems while retaining guarantees in both adversarial and stochastic environments. These settings demand different kinds of adaptability: a learner must remain reliable when outcomes are hostile while benefiting when the environment has favorable statistical structure. The goal is to combine both properties with model selection.

Each base learner supplies a candidate regret bound, which is allowed to be incorrect. A meta algorithm schedules the learners so their proposed bounds remain balanced until evidence indicates that a guarantee has been violated. Specially designed misspecification tests connect this selection process with the ability to exploit a potentially benign environment.

For adversarial environments, the resulting model selection guarantees recover those of CORRAL while adding high-probability regret bounds. The guarantees also apply simultaneously to stochastic environments under gap assumptions. That qualification matters: the stochastic result relies on the stated structure. The contribution is a theoretical framework showing that contextual-bandit model selection and these two forms of regret protection can coexist.
neurips-2022-best-of-both-worlds-model-s.tldr: A meta algorithm selects among bandit learners while providing simultaneous high-probability adversarial and, under gap assumptions, stochastic regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph classifiers can be attacked by changing graph topology. Existing robustness certificates described in this paper measure such changes through local and global edge counts. The authors argue that counting edits misses important structural properties, including isomorphism: graphs can retain the same underlying structure despite differences in how their nodes are identified.

The proposed approach measures perturbations using the orthogonal Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy. To make this structural measure usable in convex optimization, the authors construct its Fenchel biconjugate. Their mathematical development draws on a matching loss whose root relates two variables through a monotone operator. This yields a tight outer convex approximation for resistance distances between graph nodes.

The work develops both a robustness certificate and an attack algorithm within this framework. Applied to graph classification with graph convolutional networks, both are demonstrated to be effective. The contribution is therefore twofold: it changes how allowed graph perturbations are measured and supplies optimization machinery for evaluating robustness under that measure. Its central motivation is to account for structure that edge-edit totals alone overlook.
neurips-2022-certifying-robust-graph-cla.tldr: The paper develops graph robustness certificates and attacks using a structural discrepancy that goes beyond counting edge changes.

paragraphs: FinRL-Meta addresses the infrastructure needed to study reinforcement learning in financial markets. The paper identifies three obstacles to reliable environments and benchmarks: weak signals amid noisy financial data, survivorship bias in historical records, and overfitting to backtests. These problems make preparing and evaluating learning systems a substantial part of the research challenge.

The library follows a DataOps approach, using an automated curation pipeline to turn changing real-market datasets into gym-style environments. The authors describe plans to provide hundreds of these environments. They also reproduce popular research papers, giving users starting points for developing trading strategies rather than requiring every experiment to begin with a new implementation.

Cloud deployment supports visualization and relative performance assessment through community competitions. A curriculum containing tens of Jupyter and Python demonstrations, together with documentation, helps users work with the library. The contribution is an openly accessible research platform combining data preparation, environments, reproduced methods, and teaching material. Its stated purpose is to support financial reinforcement learning research; the abstract does not present a claim of profitable trading.
neurips-2022-finrl-meta-market-environme.tldr: FinRL-Meta combines automated market-data curation, reinforcement learning environments, reproduced research, and educational resources in an open financial research platform.

paragraphs: Ensembles sampled from a Bayesian posterior can help estimate uncertainty and generalize from limited data, but storing and running many models remains expensive. Functional Ensemble Distillation asks how to transfer an ensemble's predictions into an efficient model. The aim is to retain useful predictive behavior while reducing the burden of using the ensemble at test time.

The authors identify two obstacles. Existing distillation approaches are constrained to classification and the Dirichlet distribution. Moreover, when data are scarce, ensemble members can all fit the training set almost perfectly. Their predictions then look nearly identical on those examples, leaving the distillation process with little information about how the members differ.

The proposed FED approach is designed to be more general, and the paper investigates how to train it effectively in this setting. A simple mixup augmentation scheme substantially improves the distilled model's performance. Across several evaluated tasks, FED achieves better accuracy and uncertainty estimation than existing approaches. The results highlight that the examples used to teach a distilled model matter alongside the distillation formulation itself.
neurips-2022-functional-ensemble-distill.tldr: Functional Ensemble Distillation uses a general distillation approach and mixup augmentation to improve efficient models' accuracy and uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Formal neural network verification seeks to establish properties such as robustness, correctness, or safety. Bound propagation combined with branch and bound is an effective approach, but existing formulations cannot accommodate general cutting-plane constraints. These constraints strengthen convex relaxations, making the mathematical bounds used during verification more informative.

GCP-CROWN generalizes bound propagation to accept arbitrary cutting planes, including constraints involving relaxed integer variables absent from earlier formulations. This makes it possible to combine general cutting-plane techniques with efficient, GPU-accelerated bound propagation. As a case study, the authors use an off-the-shelf mixed integer programming solver to generate strong constraints.

The two components can work in parallel: the GPU-based procedure explores branches while the CPU-based solver develops cutting planes. Experiments report that GCP-CROWN completely solves oval20 and verifies twice as many oval21 instances as the best VNN-COMP 2021 tool. It also improves performance across a wider benchmark collection. The findings show how stronger mathematical relaxations and complementary hardware use can jointly improve verification.
neurips-2022-general-cutting-planes-for-.tldr: GCP-CROWN strengthens GPU-based neural network verification by incorporating general cutting planes, producing substantial gains on reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained in a limited set of environments can perform well in unseen ones. A central difficulty is separating stable predictive information from spurious features whose usefulness changes across environments. Although distribution-matching methods have empirical success, the paper notes that formal guarantees have been lacking.

Under a variant of an existing data model, the authors show that empirical risk minimization and invariant risk minimization can fail to recover the optimal invariant predictor when the number of environments is sublinear in the spurious-feature dimension. This gives a concrete setting in which having too few training environments obstructs those methods.

The proposed iterative feature matching algorithm has a stronger guarantee in that model: with high probability, it finds the optimal invariant predictor using only a logarithmic number of environments in the spurious dimension. The result is conditional on the modeled setting, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary distribution shifts. Its significance is to provide a theoretical explanation for how distribution matching can reduce the environment requirements of invariant prediction.
neurips-2022-iterative-feature-matching-.tldr: Under a specified data model, iterative feature matching recovers an optimal invariant predictor with only logarithmically many training environments.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning often shares one policy or value network across agents to reduce training cost. In tasks requiring different abilities, however, indiscriminate sharing can encourage similar behavior and weaken exploration. LDSA addresses the tension between efficient shared learning and the behavioral diversity needed for specialized subtasks.

The framework first encodes each subtask's identity as a vector. An ability-based selection strategy then dynamically groups agents with similar abilities into the same subtask. Agents assigned together share learning relevant to that role, while different subtasks support different abilities. This provides a structured way to decide where sharing should occur.

Two regularizers support the assignment process. One encourages subtask representations to differ; the other discourages frequent switching, helping stabilize training. Experiments on StarCraft II micromanagement and Google Research Football report effective assignments, better collaboration, and significantly improved learning performance. The contribution is a learned organization of the team: specialization can change during training while preserving useful sharing among agents working on the same kind of problem.
neurips-2022-ldsa-learning-dynamic-subta.tldr: LDSA dynamically groups cooperative agents by ability so they can share learning within subtasks while developing distinct specializations.

paragraphs: World models learn to predict future observations so that agents can plan by imagining action outcomes. This paper focuses on environments containing many objects, where earlier world-model successes had been difficult to extend. Its starting observation is that, even in a crowded environment, relatively few objects may be moving or interacting at any one time.

Variational Sparse Gating builds this sparse-interaction assumption into a world model learned from pixels. Stochastic binary gates control which dimensions of the model's internal feature representation update. The architecture therefore gives the latent dynamics a way to change selected features rather than updating every dimension indiscriminately at each transition.

The authors also introduce Simple Variational Sparse Gating, which removes the deterministic pathway used in previous models and makes the transition function fully stochastic. Both architectures are evaluated in BringBackShapes, an environment with many moving objects and partial observability. The reported improvements over prior models support sparse latent updates as a useful modeling bias for this setting, including when the agent cannot observe the complete environment.
neurips-2022-learning-robust-dynamics-th.tldr: Stochastic gates that selectively update latent features improve pixel-based world models in a many-object, partially observable environment.

paragraphs: Data poisoning attacks alter training examples to damage a learned model. This paper proposes a relationship between resistance to such attacks and the amount of clean data needed for accurate learning. Its Lethal Dose Conjecture says that if accurate prediction requires n clean examples, a training set of size N can tolerate poisoning on the order of N/n examples while retaining accuracy.

The authors verify the conjecture theoretically in multiple cases and develop a broader interpretation through distribution discrimination. It remains a conjecture in general. If it holds, Deep Partition Aggregation and Finite Aggregation are asymptotically optimal when supplied with the most data-efficient learner. These defenses combine votes from models trained on different training subsets.

This conditional result suggests a practical research direction: improve base learners' data efficiency to strengthen poisoning defenses. As a proof of concept, changing data augmentation doubles DPA's certified robustness on CIFAR-10 and triples it on GTSRB without sacrificing accuracy. Those experiments illustrate the proposed connection without constituting a general proof of the conjecture.
neurips-2022-lethal-dose-conjecture-on-d.tldr: The Lethal Dose Conjecture links poisoning tolerance to clean-data efficiency, with theoretical support in several cases and stronger empirical defenses.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular record was used to train a model. This paper studies that privacy question for multimodal systems whose inputs and outputs have different forms, such as image-captioning models. That setting differs from attacks on classifiers because the attacker must relate information across modalities rather than examine a conventional class prediction.

The proposed M4I framework contains two attacks. The metric-based version uses similarity measures to infer whether a target example belonged to the training data. The feature-based version uses a pretrained shadow multimodal feature extractor, comparing similarities between extracted input and output features. Both approaches use cross-modal relationships as evidence of membership.

The experiments report average attack success rates of 72.5% for the metric-based method and 94.83% for the feature-based method under unrestricted scenarios. Those conditions are part of the reported result, so the figures should be interpreted within that setting. The authors also evaluate multiple defenses. The work demonstrates a privacy risk associated with training-data membership in models that connect different types of information.
neurips-2022-m-4-i-multi-modal-models-me.tldr: Two M4I attacks use cross-modal similarities to infer training-data membership, achieving strong reported success under unrestricted scenarios.

paragraphs: This paper studies auctions when only an unknown random fraction of potential buyers participates. The setting includes multiple items, multiple bidders, and limited supply. The objective is to preserve revenue despite market shrinkage and uncertainty while maintaining truthful auctions, so that the mechanism does not depend on bidders benefiting from misreporting their preferences.

The authors introduce a formal model and a general reduction that turns a sufficiently rich auction class into a randomized auction robust to shrinkage. Their main tool is a winner diagram, a compact combinatorial representation of the possible ways an auction can run when the participating bidder set is uncertain.

A probabilistic analysis of these diagrams establishes that a sufficiently rich auction class contains a robust auction. The condition on the class is essential to this existence result. The framework also applies to practical constraints such as limiting the number of winners. Finally, the authors show how sample-based learning and efficient winner-determination routines can be used to learn a shrinkage-robust auction, connecting the theoretical guarantee to a computational approach.
neurips-2022-maximizing-revenue-under-ma.tldr: Winner diagrams enable conditional revenue-preservation guarantees and efficient learning of truthful auctions under uncertain market participation.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from a fixed collection of logged experience without continually collecting new interactions. A learned policy may choose actions unlike those taken by the behavior policy that generated the data. Their estimated values can then become overly optimistic. The paper argues that existing safeguards often go too far, suppressing useful generalization along with erroneous estimates.

Mildly Conservative Q-learning addresses this balance by assigning suitable pseudo Q values to out-of-distribution actions and actively training on those targets. Instead of relying only on penalties for unseen actions or restrictions toward the behavior policy, it gives the value function explicit training signals for those actions.

The authors theoretically show that MCQ produces a policy performing at least as well as the behavior policy and avoids erroneous overestimation of out-of-distribution actions. Experiments on D4RL report strong performance relative to prior work. The method also shows better generalization when moving from offline training to online interaction, significantly outperforming the evaluated baselines. Together, the results support calibrating conservatism to preserve opportunities for improvement.
neurips-2022-mildly-conservative-q-learn.tldr: MCQ trains unseen actions with pseudo Q targets to balance protection against overestimation with better offline reinforcement learning generalization.

paragraphs: Complex queries over knowledge graphs require several reasoning steps, often combining relationships with logical operations. Missing graph facts and errors propagated through intermediate steps make this difficult. The paper argues that earlier query-embedding approaches focus too heavily on final answers and underuse intermediate entities that could help control cascading errors.

ENeSy combines neural and symbolic reasoning so that each can support the other. Its projection operator can use any embedding method capable of link prediction. Other first-order logical operators are handled without parameters. This design separates the choice of a predictive embedding method from the machinery for operations such as union, intersection, and negation.

The framework retains both neural and symbolic reasoning results and combines them when answering queries. This is intended to address graph incompleteness alongside errors accumulated during reasoning. On complex query-answering benchmarks, ENeSy achieves state-of-the-art results, with particularly strong performance when training uses only the link-prediction task. The findings support incorporating intermediate symbolic information while preserving flexibility in the neural model used to predict relationships.
neurips-2022-neural-symbolic-entangled-f.tldr: ENeSy combines neural link prediction with symbolic reasoning to improve complex knowledge-graph queries, especially when trained only on link prediction.

paragraphs: Softmax policy gradients simplify policy optimization by avoiding a projection step after each update. In multi-agent settings, however, independently learning agents create additional convergence difficulties. There can be several Nash equilibria even when interests coincide, and softmax parameterization can produce zero-gradient policies that are not equilibria. A stationary gradient therefore does not automatically resolve the strategic problem.

The paper analyzes finite-time convergence in Markov potential games, a structured family that includes identical-interest games. It considers both ordinary gradient play and natural gradient play, with and without log-barrier regularization. The focus is on decentralized learning, where agents update without central coordination.

For unregularized methods, the convergence rates include a constant determined by the learning trajectory that can become arbitrarily large. Log-barrier regularization removes this drawback, at the cost of slightly worse dependence on other quantities, including action-set size. An experiment on an identical-interest matrix game supports the theoretical findings. The result clarifies a specific tradeoff between regularization and the factors controlling convergence speed.
neurips-2022-on-the-global-convergence-r.tldr: Log-barrier regularization removes an arbitrarily large trajectory-dependent factor from decentralized softmax convergence bounds in Markov potential games.

paragraphs: Online decision mediation places a learning assistant between a fallible decision maker and an expert. At each step, the assistant can accept the proposed action, replace it, or ask the expert. The problem is to learn when each response is worthwhile while simultaneously making decisions, rather than assuming that a useful mediation policy already exists.

The feedback structure creates a distinctive tradeoff. Asking the expert avoids error in the formalized setting and reveals an otherwise hidden expert action that becomes training data, but it also incurs an immediate penalty. An expert request can therefore affect both the present decision and the quality of future decisions.

The proposed solution weighs immediate losses against future improvements in generalization error. The authors also explain why conventional bandit algorithms may fail to address this combination. Experiments and sensitivity analyses across multiple datasets show consistent gains over applicable benchmarks, measured at the levels of the mediator policy, learned model, and overall decision system. The contribution is a framework for learning selective intervention while accounting for the future value of expert feedback.
neurips-2022-online-decision-mediation-a.tldr: Online decision mediation learns when to accept, override, or seek expert advice by balancing immediate costs against future learning benefits.

paragraphs: PDEBench provides a common testing ground for machine learning models of physical systems that evolve over time. Its tasks are defined by partial differential equations. The motivation is that scientific machine learning needs benchmarks that remain convenient to use while covering a broad range of genuinely challenging simulation problems.

The suite combines ready-to-use datasets with code for generating data and running baseline methods. It covers more kinds of equations and larger datasets than earlier benchmarks described by the authors, with simulation runs spanning varied initial conditions, boundary conditions, and equation parameters. Included methods support comparisons with classical numerical simulations and established machine learning approaches.

A standardized interface lets researchers extend the benchmark for their own purposes while keeping comparisons with existing methods accessible. The authors also introduce evaluation metrics intended to give a broader picture of model performance than existing assessment alone provides. Applying those metrics reveals tasks that remain difficult for recent learning methods. PDEBench therefore contributes both reusable infrastructure and concrete challenges for improving scientific machine learning.
neurips-2022-pdebench-an-extensive-bench.tldr: PDEBench combines diverse physical simulation datasets, extensible code, baselines, and evaluation metrics to test scientific machine learning models.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning depends heavily on how well an agent represents its state. Auxiliary losses provide additional training objectives that can help build informative representations, but designing them usually requires expert judgment. This paper asks whether a search procedure can discover useful objectives instead of relying entirely on handcrafted choices.

Automated Auxiliary Loss Search defines a space of 7.5 × 10^20 possible auxiliary losses using collected trajectory data. It explores that space with an efficient evolutionary search strategy. The contribution is a systematic way to choose representation-learning objectives from a very large set of candidates, linking that choice to reinforcement learning performance.

The discovered objective, called A2-winner, significantly improves reported performance and efficiency on unseen tasks with both image observations and vector observations. Its results also suggest promising transfer across settings and benchmark domains. A statistical analysis examines how patterns in auxiliary losses relate to learning performance. These findings support automated objective design as a route to reusable representation learning, while the generalization claim remains grounded in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2022-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: A2LS searches a large space of auxiliary objectives and discovers a loss that improves reinforcement learning across unseen image and vector tasks.

paragraphs: Many action-recognition datasets emphasize long activities, but some applications need to distinguish individual movements lasting less than a second. Stroke rehabilitation is one example: counting repetitions requires identifying these brief actions accurately. StrokeRehab introduces a benchmark designed around that finer temporal resolution rather than treating an entire daily activity as one action.

The dataset combines video and inertial sensor recordings from 51 people with stroke-related impairment and 20 healthy participants performing daily activities. Its short elemental actions have high-resolution labels. Including both groups also supports studying distribution shift, since an action-recognition model can encounter different movement patterns across the represented populations.

When tested on StrokeRehab, existing action-segmentation models produce noisy predictions that reduce action-sequence accuracy. The authors propose a speech-recognition-inspired sequence-to-sequence approach that predicts the action sequence directly. It outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods on StrokeRehab and on 50Salads, Breakfast, and Jigsaws. The paper thus pairs a dataset exposing a specific recognition challenge with a modeling approach that improves sequence identification in the reported evaluations.
neurips-2022-strokerehab-a-benchmark-dat.tldr: StrokeRehab benchmarks brief movements using video and sensor data, and a sequence-to-sequence model improves identification of action sequences.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can train solvers for combinatorial optimization with less reliance on specialized heuristics or labeled solutions. Sym-NCO asks how shared symmetries of problems and their solutions can improve that training. Rotational and reflectional invariance are examples of structure that a learned solver can use across instances of the same problem class.

The method adds regularization that uses these symmetries during training. Its purpose is to improve generalization by encouraging the solver to exploit structure shared across equivalent problem forms. This supplies a training signal based on symmetry without requiring problem-specific expert knowledge of how to construct a good solution.

Experiments report substantial improvements on traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, prize-collecting traveling salesman, and orienteering tasks. On prize-collecting traveling salesman, Sym-NCO outperforms both existing reinforcement-learning-based methods and a competitive iterative local search solver, with a reported 240-fold speed advantage over that conventional solver. The speed result belongs to that specific comparison. More broadly, the experiments support symmetry-aware regularization as a useful addition to learned optimization.
neurips-2022-sym-nco-leveraging-symmetri.tldr: Sym-NCO uses symmetry-based regularization to improve learned combinatorial solvers across four tasks, with a large reported speed advantage in one comparison.

paragraphs: Entity linking connects a mention in text to the entity it refers to in a knowledge base. Static benchmarks keep the target knowledge base fixed, but real entities change and new ones appear. TempEL is designed to measure how those temporal changes affect linking systems rather than evaluating only against a frozen collection.

The dataset uses English Wikipedia snapshots spanning 2013 through 2022. For each snapshot, it collects entity mentions and target descriptions. It includes both entities present throughout the period and entities that first appear later. This separates changes to familiar entities and their contexts from the challenge of linking entities absent when a model was trained.

Experiments with state-of-the-art linking models find temporal accuracy decreases of up to 3.1% for continual entities and up to 17.9% for new entities. These are reported maxima, not uniform losses for every model or entity. The difference highlights newly emerging entities as a particularly difficult part of temporal evaluation. TempEL makes both forms of change available for studying entity disambiguation over time.
neurips-2022-tempel-linking-dynamically-.tldr: TempEL tracks entity linking across Wikipedia snapshots and reveals larger reported temporal accuracy losses for newly emerging entities.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to improve image classification when training data are scarce. Architectures with large numbers of weights often rely on massive datasets, motivating a simpler route for small-data settings. The authors augment modern convolutional neural networks with fully connected layers and investigate how that change affects generalization.

The extra layers are useful during training, but the paper also develops an online joint knowledge-distillation method that avoids retaining them at test time. This allows the trained convolutional model to benefit from the augmented architecture without increasing its inference-time parameter count. The distinction between training architecture and deployed architecture is central to the proposed framework.

Classification experiments span multiple network backbones and standard datasets, covering supervised and active learning. The augmented training approach significantly outperforms corresponding networks without fully connected layers. In supervised learning, the reported relative validation-accuracy improvement reaches up to 16%, with no additional inference parameters. The findings show that a simple architectural addition during learning can improve small-data generalization while preserving the deployed model's weight count.
neurips-2022-the-unreasonable-effectiven.tldr: Adding fully connected layers during training and distilling their benefit improves small-data CNN accuracy without adding inference-time parameters.

paragraphs: Evaluating model explanations with people is expensive, so user studies often compare only a few explanation methods or settings. This paper introduces Simulated Evaluations, or SimEvals, to help screen those choices before a human study. The focus is whether the information an explanation provides is useful for a particular downstream task.

A SimEval trains an algorithmic agent on the information that would be shown to a user, including model explanations. The agent learns to answer questions relevant to the use case. Its test accuracy measures how predictive that information is for the task, providing a computational way to compare candidate study designs.

The authors evaluate forward simulation, model debugging, and counterfactual reasoning. Across these three use cases, the results show that SimEvals can identify explanation methods that help humans. This provides evidence for using simulated evaluations to narrow choices such as which explanations to present. The proposed role is to guide the design of potentially costly user studies by assessing task-relevant information before recruiting participants.
neurips-2022-use-case-grounded-simulatio.tldr: SimEvals use trained algorithmic agents to screen explanation methods for specific use cases before conducting costly human studies.

paragraphs: Feature selection aims to identify informative inputs within a dataset. Neural methods can perform well, but finding those inputs may require many training iterations, making large datasets or high-dimensional inputs costly to process. This paper introduces an unsupervised sparse-autoencoder method intended to find useful features much earlier in training.

Its central mechanism adapts the network's sparse topology, meaning the pattern of connections that are present. An attention-based training algorithm changes that structure to focus quickly on informative features. The proposed efficiency gain therefore comes from optimizing where the sparse model connects and directs attention during learning.

Experiments cover ten datasets spanning images, speech, text, artificial data, and biology. They include varied feature dimensions and training-set sizes. The authors report better informative-feature selection than state-of-the-art methods while substantially reducing training iterations and computational cost. They also report robustness in extremely noisy environments. These findings support learning the sparse connection pattern as a way to improve both the quality and speed of unsupervised feature selection across the tested data types.
neurips-2022-where-to-pay-attention-in-s.tldr: An attention-guided sparse autoencoder adapts its connections to select informative features faster and more accurately across ten tested datasets.
